children: is facing a fresh regulatory headache in Europe after a German court held the company liable for fraudulent third-party advertisements on Facebook and Instagram, potentially raising the bar for how quickly digital platforms must respond to reported scams.
The case was brought by a German financial portal and its founder after their trademarked logo and image were used without permission to promote allegedly fraudulent investments.
According to the court, the portal reported nearly 260 violations to Meta in August 2024 alone, with some flagged content taking as long as 62 days to be removed.
The ruling ordered Meta to remove the advertisements and pay damages.
More importantly, the court rejected Meta's attempt to rely on the Digital Services Act's lack-of-knowledge defense.

The court argued that Meta exercises meaningful control over what users see because Facebook and Instagram use algorithms to distribute content and advertisements, rather than simply displaying posts chronologically.
It cited a June European Court of Justice ruling as precedent.

Meta said it disagrees with the decision and is considering its next steps. The company also pointed to systems it already uses to proactively detect harmful content and remove material reported by users.
The September 16 decision is not final and can still be appealed.
Meta must also disclose information about the fraudulent advertisements and the revenue generated from them.
The immediate financial impact appears limited, but the precedent could matter more than the damages themselves.

If courts increasingly hold platforms responsible for fraudulent advertisements because algorithms determine who sees them, Meta could face higher compliance costs and greater legal exposure across Europe.
That could require faster review systems, additional moderation spending and tighter controls around advertiser verification.
The risk is especially relevant because advertising remains Meta's core revenue engine.
At the same time, the ruling is still appealable, so investors should avoid treating it as a settled Europe-wide standard.
The key issue is whether this reasoning spreads. A broader shift toward platform liability could make ad safety a more expensive part of Meta's business model.

title: Meta Platform Gets Blunt Court Warning Over Fraudulent Ads
